item.title: JD Vance: From Trump critic to vice president | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
From hillbilly to the White House: J. D. Vance’s rise to become Trump’s vice-president is seen by many as symbolic of a worrying trend in the US that’s further polarizing society.
J. D. Vance’s story is the story of an America that has long felt overlooked. An America of the white working class, marked by economic decline, the opioid crisis and the aftermath of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. An America that fears losing even the little that it still holds on to, through migration and social upheaval. J. D. Vance has undergone a remarkable transformation: from a fierce critic of Donald Trump to a loyal supporter of the MAGA movement and, ultimately, Trump’s vice-president. As far as his supporters are concerned, it is a career trajectory that gives him credibility. Critics, on the other hand, see in his politics a dynamic that could upset the political balance in the US and endanger democracy. Some already regard him as a potential contender for the presidency.

item.title: Hotel hope - Where refugees begin a new life | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
An integration experiment, in the heart of Germany: Refugees move into a vacant hotel, where they receive targeted support. The aim is for them to find work or a training placement, ultimately fostering a successful integration.
An empty hotel in downtown Düsseldorf is ready for a new idea. Karin Jungjohann has one - and isn’t afraid to experiment.
"What do people need most, no matter where they come from? A sense of hope for the future," said Karin Jungjohann, one of the founders of the Düsseldorf language school "Hispi". For years, she had observed how refugees in accommodation centers struggle to progress in their lives. At the same time, she was being approached by restaurateurs in Düsseldorf looking for people to fill jobs in the catering industry. This gave rise to the idea for a project designed to rethink the accommodation, support and integration of refugees: the House of Friends.
A film crew follows the initiator of the integration experiment from the initial selection of participants, through to their successful integration into the labor market and society.

item.title: Modern slavery at sea? | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Human rights abuses have been reported in the tuna industry, with working conditions described by some as modern slavery. This forced labor has also been linked to illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing practices.
Officially, these fishing boats in the Indian Ocean are fishing for tuna. But sailors say they also illegally catch endangered species. They cut off the fins of sharks to sell them at high prices and dump the live animals back into the ocean.
NGOs and advocates are pushing for tougher regulations to stop poor working conditions, but enforcing labor laws at sea remains a major challenge.

item.title: The Shuttle Disaster That Almost Grounded NASA's Dreams | Full Episode 1 | Once Upon a Time in Space
item.author: PBS
item.content:encoded:
Watch more from this series: https://to.pbs.org/4eO25vC At the height of the Cold War, the Soviet Union dominates the space race with a series of firsts, until the U.S. lands the first men on the moon in 1969. With the dawn of the Space Shuttle in 1976, the U.S. gains further ground on its rivals. In 1978, Ron McNair, Anna Fisher and Mike Mullane are among the group selected by NASA to fly aboard the Shuttle after the agency encouraged aspiring astronauts of all genders and racial backgrounds to apply.
Growing up under segregation in South Carolina, McNair had few role models for a life in space beyond Lieutenant Uhura of Star Trek. Vietnam veteran Mullane arrives at NASA skeptical that women or civilians could possess “the right stuff.” Emergency physician Fisher is thrust into the spotlight as the first mother in space. Her decision to leave her one-year-old daughter to fly into space intensifies the scrutiny.
As pressure mounts on the Shuttle program to meet military and commercial demands, disaster strikes in 1986 when Challenger explodes during launch, killing all seven astronauts. While the remaining U.S. shuttle fleet is grounded, the Soviet Union successfully launches Mir, the most sophisticated space station ever seen, and edges ahead in the space race.

item.title: Alice Roberts On The Origins of Christianity
item.author: History Hit
item.content:encoded:
Dan is joined by author, broadcaster and historian Professor Alice Roberts to examine how Christianity out-organised and outlasted the Roman Empire.
Around 50 CE, a small group of travellers began to preach that a Jewish man, crucified by the Romans, had risen from the dead. Teaching love, forgiveness and eternal life, this new faith quickly gained followers. By the early fourth century, it was thriving, and over the next hundred years, it exploded, spreading across the entire Roman Empire before becoming its official religion. What enabled it to take such a strong hold so quickly and so steadfastly?

item.title: Assaults in the hospital - When doctors harass their female colleagues | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Women who become doctors choose their profession to heal people. But in hospitals, they often become victims of sexual harassment. This film features case studies from Switzerland.
From obscene jokes by powerful bosses in the operating room to sexual blackmail and assaults during training: in this film, female students, doctors, and surgeons recount what they have had to endure. In an environment still marked by a culture of silence, harassers are rarely punished by their superiors. Often, victims are reluctant to file a complaint for fear of jeopardizing their careers. Some take the risk and report the incidents to human resources, but these complaints are seldom followed up. Although hospitals claim to have a zero-tolerance policy, harassers rarely experience any negative consequences.

item.title: India’s internet war
item.author: Vox
item.content:encoded:
In 2014, Narendra Modi pioneered the use of social media and digital campaigning in India to become prime minister. Known as one of the first global politicians to harness the power of the internet, he has the most social media followers of any world leader currently in office.
Today, over a decade since Modi’s digital-first political campaign, an internet-fueled youth movement called the Cockroach Janta Party (or the Cockroach People’s Party) is using the same social media platforms to organize protests, successfully forcing the resignation of one of Prime Minister Modi’s top advisers. The Indian government has responded with a crackdown, arresting protesters and increasingly censoring X, Meta, and other social meda sites. The legacy of the Cockroach Janta Party will be complex: on one hand, it brought to the forefront important conversations around Gen Z unemployment and meritocracy; on the other, it may have pushed the Indian government to create stricter new censorship laws to silence future dissent.
The internet that helped propel Modi to power is becoming a tool that a new generation uses against him. How much further will Modi’s government go to censor its people and restrict free speech?

ABSTRACT How do you evolve a framework over nearly two decades without losing the trust of millions of developers? In this talk, I will reflect on 19 years of working on Spring, the Java application framework—from the early days of XML configuration, through the rise of annotations, to the advent of functional programming.
I will share the lessons that come not just from designing APIs and writing code, but from practicing open source stewardship over time. That includes how to innovate under constraints, how to evolve APIs responsibly, how to serve a growing community, and why empathy and restraint are essentials skills when it comes to maintaining open source.
This talk is for anyone willing to learn from my past mistakes, so they can make entirely new ones. [...]

item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
As Apple turns 50, this film tells the story of the tech company that revolutionized our world, along with its opportunities and downsides. Has this tool of liberation become an instrument of control?
Founded 50 years ago, Apple grew from a counterculture movement into a global corporation. The film looks back at the breathtaking rise of headstrong visionary Steve Jobs, who never gave up on his dream despite fierce competition, his destructive perfectionism and even his ousting from his own company. Colleagues and companions shine light on the expertise behind Apple: designer Hartmut Esslinger created Apple's legendary 'Snow White' design language, and typographer Erik Spiekermann developed groundbreaking typefaces. People like Daniel Kottke, a former flat mate of Steve Jobs and one of the first Apple employees, share insights into the inner workings of the legendary team. Andy Cunningham, who was sacked by Jobs a total of five times, also weighs in.

item.title: The Strange Story of America’s First “Alien Abduction”
item.author: Weird History
item.content:encoded:
During a late-night drive through rural New Hampshire in 1961, Barney and Betty Hill reported a terrifying encounter with a UFO that would change their lives forever. Since then, their story remains one of the most famous and controversial alien abduction cases in history. From unexplained missing time and hypnotic regression to eerie eyewitness testimony, the Hills' account helped shape modern beliefs about extraterrestrials, UFO sightings, and even the mysteries surrounding Area 51. But were they telling the truth, or did something else happen that night?
In this episode of Weird History Presents: Graveyard Shift, we explore the shocking details behind America's first widely publicized alien abduction case, the evidence that still fuels debate decades later, and why the Barney and Betty Hill story continues to captivate believers and skeptics alike.

item.title: How a Mexican Migrant Farmer’s Journey to the U.S. Turned Fatal (full documentary) | FRONTLINE/World
item.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
item.content:encoded:
The tragic story of a migrant farmer’s journey to the U.S. in the scorching heat. (Aired June 2004)
This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb
And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate
In “Mexico: A Death in the Desert,” which aired in June 2004, correspondent Claudine LoMonaco documented the story of one migrant worker’s life and death.
Like many men from Oaxaca, Mexico, Matias Juan Garcia Zavaleta crossed the U.S.-Mexico border regularly each spring to work in California during harvest time and returned in the fall. He used his earnings to build a home and take care of his family. After years of annual crossings, Garcia had had enough of leaving his family, so he planted his own chili pepper crop. But when an early frost destroyed his plants, he was left with no choice but to cross again in the spring of 2003, but this time the crossing turned fatal.
This FRONTLINE/World short documentary traced Garcia’s journey and the impact of his death on his family.
“Mexico: A Death in the Desert” was reported and produced by Mary Spicuzza and Claudine LoMonaco. It was produced in association with UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism. The founder and executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.

The series completed its final broadcast season in 2010.
